Perceived missed-payment risk: read the survey and fund the full minimum due

Five charts explain the Bank of Canada’s perceived missed-payment probability, percentage-point changes and an independent cash example in which a later receipt cannot fund an earlier deadline.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read the survey, then fund an independently entered minimum payment

Interactive planning lab

2026 Q3 survey · interpolated median of perceived probability5.29%
Independent example · resources usable by the due day$600
Independent example · unfunded portion of the full minimum$900

The first two panels use or derive from the published overall CSCE perceived probability of missing one required minimum debt payment over the next three months. Five quarterly observations, 2025 Q3–2026 Q3, were retrieved 25 October 2026. The latest report was released 19 October; online collection was 5–27 August and follow-up interviews were 24 August–4 September. The statistic is an interpolated median of self-assessed probabilities, not an observed arrears rate, a count of missed payments or a personal risk estimate. The methodology paper’s inversion applies to its composite financial-health index; these charts keep the raw positive probability. The remaining panels use independent fictional CAD inputs for one already-quoted payment, one dedicated opening cash amount and one cleared receipt. No survey value enters the cash arithmetic. The receipt is assumed usable before the payment on a shared day. Dates represent usable funds and the required funding deadline, not a guaranteed processing service or statutory grace period. The stepped calendar is a funding ledger: negative values identify resources missing against the full scheduled obligation, not an authorized overdraft or a claim that an unfunded payment actually cleared. No other bills, credit, interest, late fees, benefit changes, taxes or subsequent instalments are modeled. Enter net usable cash after other commitments; no amount is allocated twice.

The central idea

Read the question, summary statistic and horizon before interpreting a risk percentage. Then fund the actual minimum payment from cash usable by its deadline, without scaling the bill by a population survey result.

01

Start with the event and the horizon the respondent was asked about

A percentage beside a debt headline can describe several different things: people already behind, balances past due, or respondents’ beliefs about what might happen. The first chart concerns the last of these.

The Bank of Canada’s Canadian Survey of Consumer Expectations asks for a person’s perceived chance of being unable to make a required minimum debt payment during the next three months. The question spans several debt products. It does not ask how much of a balance is delinquent or how many payments have already been missed. The survey data page retains the question beside its observations.

The survey overview describes a rotating online panel of approximately 2,000 household heads, with an adult Canadian target population. This aggregate series does not establish a risk estimate for a particular reader.

02

Keep the interpolated median separate from a count or an average

The methodology study identifies this payment-probability component as an interpolated median. That summarizes the centre of respondents’ numerical assessments; it is not an arithmetic mean and cannot be read as the percentage who answered that they had already missed a payment.

Table A-1 of the 2025 staff discussion paper, printed page 17 and PDF page 20, also labels the component as inverted when used inside a financial-health index. That orientation makes sense within that index’s construction. This article plots the original positive probability series, without applying the index transformation.

Neither a median nor its change reveals the full response distribution. The extract supplies no respondent records, uncertainty interval or subsequent payment outcomes. It therefore cannot tell us how many individuals became safer, whether the movement is statistically significant, or how accurately these beliefs later predicted missed payments.

03

Compare probability levels without converting them into a cash reserve

The bounded overall-series extract contains five quarterly values: 5.78%, 9.49%, 9.24%, 7.37% and 5.29%, from 2025 Q3 through 2026 Q3. The latest difference is 5.29% − 7.37% = −2.08 percentage points. A relative percentage change would use a different denominator.

Each quarter retains a forward-looking three-month question. Dividing its figure by three does not identify a monthly risk, and joining the observations does not create one person’s continuous probability path.

Nor should the latest value become a funding haircut. Multiplying a known CAD 1,500 minimum by 5.29% produces CAD 79.35, but that calculation neither funds the CAD 1,500 obligation nor estimates this borrower’s expected loss. The population summary is not an entered personal probability, and even a well-supported probability would answer a different question from the cash needed for a known payment.

04

Reconcile the entire minimum against resources usable on its funding day

The independent example starts with a quoted next minimum of CAD 1,500, dedicated opening cash of CAD 600 and one additional cleared receipt of CAD 1,000. The minimum must be funded on day 10; the receipt becomes usable on day 15. These are fictional amounts and dates, chosen separately from every survey observation.

Only CAD 600 is usable by the deadline, leaving CAD 900 unfunded. The waterfall starts with the full minimum and subtracts usable resources applied to it. If available resources exceed the payment, the applied amount stops at the bill and the shortfall stops at zero. Extra cash remains outside that bill reconciliation; it is not a negative funding need.

Opening cash must already be free of other commitments. Counting money promised to rent, groceries or another debt as dedicated to this payment would overstate capacity. Likewise, the additional receipt means cash actually available after other allocations, not gross salary or an unpaid invoice. No tax or other bill is deducted again inside this isolated example.

05

A later positive balance does not repair the earlier funding gap

The stepped chart begins at CAD 600. Deducting the full scheduled payment on day 10 takes the funding ledger to minus CAD 900. Adding the receipt on day 15 takes it to plus CAD 100. That positive endpoint coexists with an earlier shortfall; it does not show that the payment was affordable when due.

The negative segment measures missing funding against the obligation. It is not a claim that a bank processed an unfunded transfer, granted an overdraft or allowed payment five days late. Fees, interest, credit consequences and any revised agreement would require separate facts.

Moving the receipt to day 10 removes the shortfall under this example’s explicit receipt-before-payment convention. The day-end plot makes no intraday guarantee. The matrix varies opening cash and usable receipt dates while keeping the selected bill, receipt amount and funding deadline. Its alternatives have no assigned probabilities; they are not forecasts generated from the survey.

06

Use the survey for context and the actual statement for the payment plan

The 2026 Q3 report was released on 19 October. Online responses were collected from 5 to 27 August, with follow-up interviews from 24 August to 4 September. These dates differ from the quarter-start keys used to label the dataset. All displayed observations come from the snapshot reviewed on 25 October 2026.

For a real payment, record the statement amount, required deadline, usable account cash and processing time. FCAC explains that payment methods and institutions affect credit-card processing. This calculator does not infer a universal grace period or determine when an issuer considers a payment received.

If funding appears insufficient, FCAC advises contacting the lender promptly. A survey improvement cannot replace that discussion. Keep the population indicator, your verified payment terms and the independently tested cash scenarios beside one another, with their different purposes clearly labelled.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Two panels use or derive from public CSCE overall observations for 2025 Q3–2026 Q3. Three panels are independent fictional CAD funding examples. The survey measures self-assessed next-three-month probabilities; it supplies neither observed arrears frequencies nor the reader’s personal default probability. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
